1910: A blowhard is a person who talks loudly and endlessly about how great, smart, knowledgeable, or important they are — but whose big talk is mostly empty air. The word captures two things at once: the volume of their talking and the hollowness behind it. Think of someone who is all bark and no bite, all show and no substance.

A blowhard:

  • Brags constantly. They talk about their own achievements, experiences, and opinions far more than any situation calls for. They find a way to make almost any conversation about themselves.
  • Exaggerates or inflates the truth. Their stories are always a little too impressive. That fish they caught keeps getting bigger every time they tell the story.
  • Acts like an authority on everything. They speak with great confidence about topics they don't actually know well. They give advice nobody asked for, and they never say "I don't know."
  • Dominates conversations. They are not really interested in listening. For them, a conversation is just an opportunity to perform.
  • Promises more than they deliver. If they say they can do something, there's a good chance they can't — or won't. Their words far outrun their actions.
The Single Most Important Thing to Understand

The heart of the word is this: there is a massive gap between what a blowhard says and what is actually true.

A confident person who backs up their words with real skill and action is not a blowhard. A person who genuinely knows a lot about a subject and shares that knowledge is not a blowhard. What makes someone a blowhard is precisely that their grand talk is not matched by reality. The louder and bigger the talk, the thinner the substance behind it.

"Blowhard" is always a negative and slightly mocking word. When you call someone a blowhard, you are not just describing them — you are criticising them and dismissing them. It carries a sense of "don't take this person too seriously." It's the kind of word people use with an eye-roll. It signals that the speaker finds the blowhard tiresome, ridiculous, or annoying.
How It Feels to Be Around a Blowhard

People find blowhards exhausting and irritating. You might feel:

  • Like you can never get a word in.
  • Bored or trapped, because the conversation goes nowhere real.
  • Slightly disrespected, because they clearly care more about talking than about you.
  • Quietly amused or contemptuous, because you can see through their exaggerations.

Over time, people stop trusting or taking blowhards seriously, even if they let them keep talking.

• "Nobody at the office believes his ideas anymore — he's just a blowhard who talks big but never follows through."
  • "She tuned him out halfway through dinner. He was such a blowhard, going on and on about how successful he was."
  • "Don't be fooled by him — he's a total blowhard. He's never actually done half the things he claims."
  • "The meeting was supposed to last an hour, but the blowhard in the corner turned it into a three-hour lecture about his own opinions."
How a Blowhard Differs From Similar Types of People

ConceptKey Difference

A liar deliberately says false things to deceive people for a specific goal. A blowhard may exaggerate and mislead too, but their primary drive is self-promotion and ego, not calculated deception.

A confident person believes in themselves and can usually back it up. A blowhard acts confident but is often masking insecurity beneath all that noise.

A loudmouth is simply someone who speaks too loudly or says inappropriate things. A blowhard is specifically about bragging and self-importance — it's more specific than just being loud.

A bore is someone who is dull and uninteresting. A blowhard can overlap with this, but the defining feature of a blowhard is the self-aggrandisement, not just the dullness.
Words That Are Close in Meaning

These words share the same spirit as "blowhard" and are worth knowing alongside it:

  • Braggart — someone who brags constantly (very close in meaning, but slightly more old-fashioned).
  • Windbag — someone who talks endlessly and says little of value (more emphasis on the length of talk, less on the bragging).
  • Boaster — someone who boasts about themselves (simpler, more neutral in tone).
  • Show-off — someone who tries to impress others by displaying their abilities or possessions (slightly less aggressive in tone than blowhard).

Of all these, blowhard is the most colourful and pointed — it combines the idea of too much hot air and too much ego in one sharp word.

If you had to boil it down to one sentence:

A blowhard is someone whose mouth is far bigger than their actual achievements — a loud, self-important talker who impresses themselves far more than they impress anyone else.

That's the word, fully understood.
1911:
"Blowing" as an adjective describes something that is being moved, carried, or driven through the air by wind — or something that is actively and noticeably producing or experiencing strong air movement.

It comes from the verb "blow," and when used as an adjective, it sits directly before a noun to describe that noun's current state of motion through air.
The main ways it is used

1. Something being carried or pushed by wind

This is the most common use. When you place "blowing" in front of a noun, it almost always means the wind has picked that thing up and is transporting it through the air.

  • blowing snow — snow that wind has lifted off the ground and is carrying through the air
  • blowing sand — grains of sand being pushed and swept by wind
  • blowing dust — fine dust lifted off the ground and moved through the air
  • blowing leaves — leaves being swept and tossed through the air by wind
  • blowing hair — hair being tossed and moved around by wind
  • blowing curtains — curtains billowing and moving because wind is pushing through them

In every case above, the word "blowing" tells you: this thing is not sitting still — wind is actively moving it.

2. Wind or air itself that is actively moving

"Blowing" can also describe wind or a force of air that is currently in action — moving, gusting, rushing.

  • a blowing wind — wind that is actively and noticeably moving at this moment
  • a blowing gale — a powerful, raging wind that is in full motion
  • a blowing breeze — a breeze that is currently flowing through the air

Here, "blowing" tells you the wind is not calm or still — it is live and in motion.

3. Anything producing a stream of air

More broadly, "blowing" can describe any source that is actively pushing or expelling air — not just natural wind, but anything that blows.

  • a blowing fan — a fan that is on and pushing air outward
  • a blowing vent — an air vent that is actively releasing air
A very important distinction — especially in weather

In weather reports and meteorology, "blowing" before certain words has a precise technical meaning worth knowing:

  • Blowing snow, blowing sand, and blowing dust are recognized weather events where wind lifts particles off the ground surface and carries them horizontally through the air, reducing visibility (how far you can see).

This is importantly different from related terms:

ConceptWhat it means
  • Falling snow means snow is coming down from clouds. Blowing snow means snow that already landed on the ground has been lifted back up by wind and is now being swept through the air again. It can be "blowing snow" even on a clear day with no snowfall, as long as wind is strong enough to pick up previously fallen snow.
  • Drifting snow stays low, near the ground, forming uneven piles (drifts). Blowing snow is lifted higher into the air, creating a hazy, white-out effect.

This distinction matters because blowing snow can be dangerous — it can reduce visibility to near zero without a single new snowflake falling from the sky.

The same logic applies to blowing dust and blowing sand: the particles are already on the ground, but powerful wind picks them up and launches them into the air.
How "blowing" is different from other similar adjectives

• Windy describes a place or time when there is a lot of wind in general: "It's a windy day." It describes the condition of the environment. "Blowing" describes something specific — a noun — that is actively being moved by that wind: "blowing leaves," "blowing sand."
  • Breezy is a softer, gentler version of windy — light, pleasant wind. "Blowing" implies more active, visible movement — something actually being lifted and carried.
  • Gusty describes wind that comes in sudden, irregular bursts. "Blowing" describes the state of something being in ongoing motion due to wind.
A note on "mind-blowing" and compound uses

You may also encounter "blowing" inside compound adjectives like mind-blowing. Here, the meaning has shifted figuratively: something that is "mind-blowing" is so surprising, impressive, or overwhelming that it figuratively "blows your mind" — it stuns you. But in this compound form, it's no longer about wind or air; it's entirely figurative. The standalone adjective "blowing" almost always connects back to the literal movement of air.
Quick mental test to recognize it

Whenever you see "blowing" before a noun, ask yourself: Is the wind — or some force of air — actively moving this thing right now? If yes, that is exactly what "blowing" is communicating. It signals live, active motion through air, rather than something calm, still, or settled.
1912: The word blowout is a single noun with several distinct meanings. Each meaning shares a common thread — something happening suddenly, forcefully, or on a very large scale. Here is every meaning explained clearly, with examples.
Meaning 1: A Tire That Suddenly Bursts

This is the most common, everyday meaning of the word.

A blowout happens when a vehicle's tire suddenly explodes or bursts while the vehicle is moving. It is not a slow, gradual loss of air — it is fast and loud, like a small explosion. This is dangerous because the driver can lose control of the vehicle.

"We were driving on the highway when we had a blowout. The car swerved and we had to pull over immediately."

"The blowout shredded the rear tire completely."

When people say "I had a blowout," most listeners immediately picture a burst tire. This meaning is used in everyday conversation all the time.
Meaning 2: A One-Sided Victory in Sports or Competition

In sports and competitive situations, a blowout refers to a game or contest where one side wins by a huge margin — so decisively that the result was never really in doubt. It is the opposite of a close, exciting match.

"The final score was 98 to 54. It was a complete blowout."

"Nobody wanted to watch the game after the first quarter — it had become a blowout."

The key idea here is that one team or side was so much stronger that the competition became almost meaningless. The word carries a slightly informal, conversational tone and is very common in sports commentary and casual talk.
Meaning 3: A Large, Lavish Party or Celebration

A blowout can also mean a big, extravagant celebration — a party or social event that is especially large, loud, or expensive. The "blow" here suggests going all-out, sparing no effort.

"They threw a massive blowout for her retirement — there were hundreds of guests and a live band."

"We're planning a real blowout for New Year's Eve this year."

This meaning is casual and positive. It suggests the event was memorable, over-the-top, or particularly lively. You often see phrases like "throw a blowout" or "have a blowout."

In the context of hair and beauty, a blowout refers to a professional hair treatment where a stylist washes your hair and then blow-dries and brushes it to make it look smooth, voluminous, and styled. No cutting involved — it is purely about styling using heat and a brush.

"She got a blowout before the wedding so her hair would look perfectly straight and shiny."

"I go to the salon every two weeks just for a blowout."

This meaning is very common, especially in American English. Many salons offer "blowouts" as a quick, affordable service compared to a full haircut appointment.
Meaning 5: An Uncontrolled Burst from an Oil or Gas Well

In the oil and gas industry, a blowout is a serious industrial accident where oil, gas, or both suddenly and violently burst out of a well in an uncontrolled way. This happens when the pressure underground is too great to be contained. Blowouts can cause fires, explosions, and major environmental disasters.

"The offshore blowout spilled millions of gallons of oil into the sea."

"Engineers worked for weeks trying to stop the blowout."

This is a technical, industry-specific meaning, but it appears often in news reporting about energy and environmental disasters.
Meaning 6: A Blown Fuse or Electrical Failure

A blowout can describe the sudden failure of an electrical component — most commonly a fuse — due to excess electricity passing through it. When a fuse blows, it cuts off the power to protect equipment. This is sometimes called a blowout because the fuse is designed to "blow" (break open) under overload.

"There was a blowout in the circuit, and half the lights in the building went dark."

"The power surge caused a blowout, and we had to replace several fuses."

This meaning is less common in daily conversation but appears in technical and household contexts.

Particularly in retail, a blowout (sometimes written as blowout sale) refers to a large sale where a store tries to sell off all its remaining inventory, often at very low prices. The goal is to "blow out" (clear out) all the stock quickly.

"The store is closing down — everything is half price in the blowout sale."

"They're having a blowout on last season's electronics."

This meaning is common in advertising and retail contexts.

Even though the contexts differ wildly — tires, sports, parties, hair, oil wells — the word blowout always suggests something happening in a big, sudden, or extreme way. A tire doesn't slowly deflate — it blows out violently. A sports result isn't close — it's overwhelmingly one-sided. A party isn't modest — it's extravagant. This shared sense of "excessive force or scale" is the invisible thread running through all uses of the word.

• Someone talking about driving → burst tire
  • Someone talking about a game or match → one-sided result
  • Someone talking about a party or event → big celebration
  • Someone talking about hair → blow-dry styling session
  • Someone talking about oil or energy → uncontrolled well eruption
  • Someone talking about electricity → blown fuse or power failure
  • Someone talking about shopping → clearance sale
1913:
Blubber is the thick, soft layer of fat that sits just beneath the skin of certain sea animals — most famously whales, but also seals, walruses, and dolphins.

Think of it like a built-in coat. Just as you wear a thick winter jacket to survive freezing cold weather, these animals have blubber wrapped all around their bodies to survive freezing cold ocean water. Except unlike your jacket, blubber is not worn — it is a part of their body, sandwiched between their outer skin and their inner muscles.

Blubber is not just any ordinary fat. It is a dense, thick, oily layer of fatty tissue. In large whales, this layer can be anywhere from a few centimetres to over 50 centimetres (nearly 20 inches) thick. If you were to cut through a whale, you would see a distinct, pale yellowish-white rubbery layer — that is the blubber.

It feels soft and greasy, much like the fat you might see around a cut of meat, but far thicker and more organised as a continuous layer all over the animal's body.

Blubber serves three major purposes, and understanding these will make the word stick in your mind forever.

1. It keeps the animal warm (insulation)
Ocean water — especially in the Arctic or deep sea — is bitterly cold. If a whale had no blubber, the cold water would drain heat from its body very quickly, just like how standing outside without a jacket in winter makes you cold fast. Blubber traps the animal's body heat inside, acting as a near-perfect insulator. The thicker the blubber, the better protected the animal is from the cold.

2. It stores energy (fuel reserve)
Fat is a form of stored energy. When a whale travels thousands of miles during migration and cannot eat for weeks or even months, its body slowly burns through its blubber for fuel — the same way a car burns through its petrol tank on a long road trip.

3. It helps the animal float (buoyancy)
Fat is lighter than muscle and bone, so blubber makes the animal slightly more buoyant (easier to float) in water. This is helpful for animals that spend their entire lives in the ocean.

Blubber forms a complete layer all around the animal's body — like a full-body suit under the skin. It covers the top, bottom, and sides, but is usually not found in the fins or tail flukes. This uniform coverage is important so that no part of the animal's body loses heat to the water.

In its most proper and common use, blubber refers specifically to this fat layer in marine (sea-dwelling) mammals. You would not usually say that a land animal like a bear or a pig has "blubber" — those animals have fat, but the word blubber is reserved for sea animals.

However, in informal, everyday conversation — especially among children or in casual speech — blubber is sometimes used to refer to excess body fat on a human being, usually in a rude or teasing way (e.g., "Look at all that blubber on him"). This usage is considered unkind and insulting. You should be aware it exists, but know that using it this way about a person is disrespectful.

For hundreds of years, people hunted whales primarily for their blubber. When blubber is boiled down, it produces a rich oil (called whale oil) that was once used as fuel in oil lamps to light homes, as a lubricant for machinery, and as an ingredient in soap and candles. This made whale blubber an extremely valuable and heavily traded commodity — before petroleum and electricity became widely available. Today, commercial whaling for blubber is banned or heavily restricted in most of the world.

What it isA thick layer of fat beneath the skin
Found inWhales, seals, walruses, dolphins, and similar sea mammals
Main jobsKeep the animal warm, store energy, aid in floating
AppearanceSoft, pale yellowish-white, oily, and dense
In informal useRudely refers to excess body fat on a person
A Sentence to Remember It By

"The whale's thick blubber kept it perfectly warm even in the icy Arctic waters, despite the temperature being just a few degrees above freezing."

After reading this, if someone mentions blubber in any context — a nature documentary, a history book about whale hunters, or even a rude playground comment — you will know exactly what it means, where it comes from, and why it matters.
1914:
To blubber means to cry loudly, messily, and in an uncontrolled way — so hard that your body shakes, your face scrunches up, your nose runs, and you can barely speak properly. It is not quiet, elegant crying. It is full-on, sloppy, gasping, heaving crying that is very hard to stop.

She blubbered for an hour after hearing the bad news.
What Makes It Different from Simply "Crying"

English has many words for crying — cry, weep, sob, wail, bawl, whimper — and they all mean slightly different things. Blubber sits at the extreme, messy end of the scale.

  • Weep → quiet, gentle, dignified tears
  • Sob → broken, uneven crying with gasps for breath
  • Bawl → loud, open-mouthed crying (often used for babies or young children)
  • Blubber → loud, sloppy, out-of-control crying where the person cannot properly compose themselves, cannot speak clearly, and looks rather undignified

The key ingredient that separates blubber from the rest is this combination: the crying is loud + messy + uncontrolled + makes speech difficult.
The Hidden Attitude Inside the Word

This is the most important thing for a learner to understand: blubber is not a neutral word.

When you use it, you are not just describing how someone is crying — you are also quietly judging or dismissing that crying as excessive, childish, self-pitying, or embarrassing. The word carries a slightly mocking or impatient tone.

Think of a frustrated parent saying to a child:

"Stop blubbering and tell me what happened."

The parent isn't being sympathetic. They find the crying over-the-top and want it to stop.

Or a friend saying:

"He blubbered through the entire movie."

Again, there's a hint of gentle ridicule — the person is crying more than the speaker thinks is reasonable.

So the rule is: if you describe someone as blubbering, you are not being kind about it. You are suggesting their crying is a bit too much.
It Can Also Mean: Saying Something While Blubbering

The verb has a second, closely related use. You can blubber something out — meaning to say something while crying so hard that the words come out broken, wet, and barely understandable.

"I'm so sorry," she blubbered, wiping her face with her sleeve.
He blubbered out an apology that nobody could quite understand.

Here, blubber works almost like the words "say" or "speak," but it tells you that the speaking was interrupted and distorted by messy, uncontrolled crying.
Register: When and Where Is This Word Used?

Blubber is an informal, everyday word. You would use it in:

  • Casual conversation with friends or family
  • Informal writing (a blog post, a personal message, a novel with a casual tone)
  • Slightly humorous or sarcastic contexts

You would not use it in:

  • Formal writing (academic papers, official reports)
  • Situations where you want to show genuine sympathy (because the word sounds dismissive)

If you say someone is blubbering…
✅ They are crying loudly and messily
✅ Their crying is uncontrolled and hard to stop
✅ They probably can't speak clearly
✅ You (the speaker) think the crying is excessive or childish
❌ It does NOT suggest quiet, dignified, or gentle crying
❌ It is NOT a sympathetic or kind description

The child blubbered all the way home after losing his balloon.

I'm not ashamed to admit I blubbered at the end of that film.

(Here, the speaker is poking fun at themselves.)

"Just stop blubbering!" his older brother snapped.

She tried to explain what had happened, but she was blubbering too hard for anyone to understand her.

In short: to blubber = to cry in a loud, messy, uncontrolled, and undignified way, and when you use this word, you are always adding a small dose of judgment that the crying is excessive. Master that, and you have fully mastered this word.
1915: A bludgeon is a heavy, thick stick used as a weapon to beat or strike someone.

Picture a wooden club — short to medium in length, roughly the size you can hold in one hand. What makes a bludgeon distinct is its shape: it is typically thicker and heavier at one end than the other. The heavier end is the striking end — the part that does damage. The narrower end is where you grip it. Think of it like an oversized, crude baseball bat, but blunter and more primitive.

It doesn't have to be wood. A bludgeon can be made of metal, rubber, or any dense, hard material. What defines it is the heaviness and the blunt, clublike quality — it is not sharp like a blade. It crushes and bruises rather than cuts.

A bludgeon is purely a weapon. Its entire purpose is to hit people (or things) with brute, crushing force. It is one of humanity's oldest weapons — simple, brutal, and effective. In historical settings, soldiers, criminals, and guards all used bludgeons. Today, you'll see the word used when describing:

  • A robber who attacks someone with a heavy stick
  • An ancient warrior wielding a war club
  • Any scene where someone is beaten with a thick, blunt object

A police officer's baton or nightstick is a close modern relative of a bludgeon — though the word "bludgeon" carries a rawer, more violent feel.

"Bludgeon" is not a neutral word. It carries a sense of brutality, crudeness, and raw force. When a writer chooses the word "bludgeon" over "stick" or "club," they are emphasizing the violent, savage nature of the weapon. It sounds heavy. It sounds brutal. That is intentional.
Figurative use (how it's used beyond the physical)

Even when no actual stick is involved, people use "bludgeon" as a noun to mean something used to overwhelm, crush, or force someone into submission — not physically, but mentally or emotionally.

For example:

  • "He used statistics as a bludgeon to silence anyone who disagreed with him."

Here, the statistics aren't a real stick — but the speaker is saying that the person wielded them like one: forcefully, bluntly, with the intent to overpower rather than persuade.

This figurative use is very common. Whenever something is used as a heavy, forceful tool to dominate rather than to reason or convince, that thing can be called a bludgeon.

• The attacker struck him with a wooden bludgeon.
  • Archaeologists found ancient bludgeons at the site, suggesting the tribe engaged in close combat.
  • Fear was the dictator's favorite bludgeon — he used it to keep people obedient.
  • The lawyer's aggressive cross-examination was less a scalpel and more a bludgeon.
How it differs from similar words

WordWhat it means
ClubThe broad, general term for a heavy stick weapon. Bludgeon is more specific — it implies something especially crude and brutal.
BatUsually associated with sport; not inherently a weapon.
Truncheon / BatonOfficial, standardized tools used by law enforcement. More controlled.
BludgeonAlways feels raw, violent, and blunt — whether used literally or figuratively.

A bludgeon is a heavy, blunt, thick stick used as a crude weapon to strike with crushing force — and by extension, anything used with that same kind of brute, overpowering force in speech, argument, or power.
1916:
To bludgeon someone means to hit them hard and repeatedly with a heavy object — or, in a figurative sense, to force or pressure someone aggressively into doing or accepting something.

Both meanings share one soul: overwhelming brute force. Not grace, not skill, not subtlety — just raw, relentless, crushing power.

When used literally, to bludgeon someone means to beat them with something heavy and blunt — a club, a pipe, a bat, or even a fist. The key qualities of this action are:

It is heavy. The force is massive, not light or delicate.

It is blunt. Unlike a knife (which cuts cleanly), bludgeoning is crude and messy. It crushes rather than pierces.

It is repeated. You don't bludgeon someone with a single tap. The word implies multiple, forceful blows delivered again and again.

Example sentences:

  • "The attacker bludgeoned the man with an iron bar and fled."
  • "The boxer bludgeoned his opponent until the referee stopped the fight."
The Figurative Meaning (Very Common in Everyday Use)

This is where the word really shines in modern usage. You can bludgeon someone without touching them at all.

To bludgeon someone figuratively means to force, pressure, or overwhelm them — through relentless arguing, aggressive behaviour, shouting, threats, or sheer persistence — until they give up and do what you want. The victim doesn't get a fair chance to think or resist. They are simply worn down or bulldozed into submission.

Think of it as the verbal or psychological equivalent of being beaten into the ground.

Example sentences:

  • "He bludgeoned his team into agreeing with his plan by refusing to listen to any objections."
  • "She felt bludgeoned by the constant criticism from her boss."
  • "The politician bludgeoned the audience with statistics until no one dared to challenge him."
  • "Stop trying to bludgeon me into changing my mind — I've made my decision."

Bludgeon is not a neutral word. It always carries a strong negative feeling. When you say someone bludgeoned another person (literally or figuratively), you are almost always expressing that:

  • The action was unfair or brutal
  • The victim was helpless or overpowered
  • The person doing it was aggressive and showed no respect for the other

If someone "persuades" you, they used reason. If someone "bludgeons" you, they used force. One respects you; the other tramples you.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Bludgeon vs. Hit: "Hit" is a single, neutral action. "Bludgeon" is repeated, heavy, and brutal. You can hit someone lightly; you cannot bludgeon someone lightly.

Bludgeon vs. Beat: "Beat" is similar but more general. "Bludgeon" specifically implies blunt, heavy force — it paints a more vivid, brutal picture.

Bludgeon vs. Bully (figurative): "Bully" is about repeated intimidation over time. "Bludgeon" is more intense and immediate — it's about overwhelming someone right now, in the moment, with sheer force.

Bludgeon vs. Persuade (figurative): "Persuade" means to change someone's mind using logic, evidence, or charm. "Bludgeon" means to change it by force. One is respectful; the other is not.

In figurative use, the word follows predictable patterns:

  • A boss bludgeons employees into accepting bad decisions.
  • A politician bludgeons opponents with aggressive rhetoric.
  • A parent might bludgeon a child into obedience through shouting.
  • A salesperson might bludgeon a customer into buying by refusing to take no for an answer.

Notice that it's almost always someone with more power, more persistence, or more aggression doing the bludgeoning.
The One Thing to Always Remember

Whenever you see or hear the word "bludgeon," think of one image: something heavy, coming down again and again, leaving no room to escape or fight back. Whether that's a physical blow or the weight of someone's pressure, manipulation, or aggression — that is what bludgeon always means.

It is the word for when force replaces fairness.
1917:
1. The Color

The most fundamental meaning of blue is a color — the color of a clear daytime sky, deep ocean water, or a sapphire gem. It is a cool, calm color.

Because blue covers a wide family of shades, modifiers are commonly added to be precise:

Lighter blues — sky blue, baby blue, powder blue, ice blue, cornflower blue, periwinkle. These are soft, delicate, airy shades.

Medium blues — cerulean, ocean blue, slate blue. These are clear, definite blues, neither pale nor deep.

Darker blues — navy blue, royal blue, cobalt blue, midnight blue, steel blue. These are rich, strong, dramatic shades.

When someone simply says "blue" without any qualifier, they usually mean a clear, medium shade — roughly the color of a calm sky on a sunny afternoon.

Nearly anything visible can be described as blue: eyes, the sky, water, ink, clothing, a car, a door, a flower, a bruise, or a vein seen through skin.

  • "She had bright blue eyes."
  • "He wore a navy blue suit to the interview."
  • "The lake looked blue under the afternoon sun."

One of the most common figurative uses of "blue" is to describe a feeling of sadness, low spirits, or mild melancholy. When someone feels blue, they feel down or gloomy — not necessarily deeply depressed, but not their usual self either.

  • "I've been feeling a bit blue since my friend moved away."
  • "Why are you so blue today? What happened?"
  • "The long grey winter made everyone blue."

This meaning is very natural and widely used in everyday English conversation, songs, and writing. You will hear it constantly.
3. Indecent, Crude, or Adult in Nature

When a joke, a film, a comedian, or language is described as blue, it means it contains sexually suggestive, crude, or vulgar content — things considered inappropriate for children or conservative audiences.

"Blue" in this sense is a polite, indirect way of labeling something as adult or risqué.

  • "His blue jokes are not suitable for the office."
  • "The comedian's routine was a bit too blue for my taste."
  • "That show has some blue language — parents, take note."

A blue movie is a pornographic film. A blue comedian is one whose material is sexually explicit or crude. Blue language means obscene or offensive words.

This meaning is very context-dependent, because "blue" means opposite things in different countries:

In the United States: Blue represents the Democratic Party. States, districts, and cities that lean Democratic are called "blue." On US election maps, blue areas vote for the center-left party.

  • "California is a solidly blue state."
  • "She represents a reliably blue congressional district."

In the United Kingdom: Blue represents the Conservative Party (the Tories). Conservative voters and strongholds are traditionally described as blue.

  • "It's a safe blue seat — the Conservatives have held it for decades."

Always pay attention to which country the speaker is from, because the political associations are quite different.

When a person's skin — especially the lips, fingertips, or face — turns a bluish color, they are described as blue. This happens in two main situations:

Cold: Extreme cold causes the blood vessels near the skin to narrow, reducing blood flow and turning the skin bluish.

  • "She was blue with cold after standing outside in the blizzard."
  • "His lips turned blue in the freezing water."

Lack of oxygen: When someone is not getting enough oxygen — due to choking, a breathing problem, or a medical emergency — their skin can turn blue. This is a sign of a serious emergency.

  • "The baby's face was turning blue — call an ambulance immediately!"

In certain legal and historical contexts, blue describes rules, laws, or people that are excessively strict about morality and proper conduct, especially concerning behavior considered sinful or indecent.

Blue laws are laws that restrict certain activities — typically commercial activities or alcohol sales — on Sundays, originally based on religious reasoning.

  • "Blue laws in this county mean stores can't sell alcohol before noon on a Sunday."

A blue-nosed person is one who is extremely prim, moralistic, and disapproving of anything they consider fun or improper.

This sense is not common in casual everyday speech, but you will encounter it in legal writing, journalism, and historical discussions.

Blue can describe someone from a noble, aristocratic, or royal family — rooted in the phrase "blue blood."

  • "She comes from a blue-blooded family with centuries of aristocratic history."
  • "He's blue blood — his ancestors were European nobles."

This meaning appears most often in formal writing, journalism about royalty, or discussions about old wealth and lineage.

Blue-collar
Describes workers who do manual, physical, or skilled trade work — factory workers, plumbers, electricians, construction workers, truck drivers. The name comes from the tradition of such workers wearing durable, often dark work uniforms. The opposite is white-collar, which describes office or professional work.

  • "This is a blue-collar town built around manufacturing."
  • "Blue-collar workers were hit hardest by the factory closures."

Blue-chip
Describes something — most commonly a company, stock, or investment — that is well-established, financially strong, highly reliable, and of the highest quality. Named after the highest-value chip in poker (traditionally blue).

  • "She only invests in blue-chip companies."
  • "It's a blue-chip firm — the most prestigious in the industry."

True blue
Means completely loyal, dependable, faithful, and genuine. A true-blue person is someone who never lets you down, stands by you through everything.

  • "He's true blue — he was there for me even in my worst times."
  • "She's a true-blue supporter of the team, win or lose."

Blue-eyed
Literally means having blue eyes. But blue-eyed boy (or blue-eyed girl) is an idiom meaning someone who is a special favorite — the person in a group who seems to get preferential treatment from people in charge.

  • "He's always been the manager's blue-eyed boy — he gets all the best assignments."

These are expressions where "blue" carries a meaning beyond its literal color sense. Learning these will make you sound very natural in English.

Once in a blue moon
Meaning: Very rarely; almost never.
(A "blue moon" refers to the second full moon in a single calendar month, which is an uncommon event.)

  • "We meet once in a blue moon, but we're still close friends."
  • "I eat fast food once in a blue moon."

Out of the blue
Meaning: Completely suddenly and unexpectedly, with no warning at all. (Picture something falling from a clear, cloudless blue sky — no storm, no warning.)

  • "She called me out of the blue after years of silence."
  • "The news came completely out of the blue — nobody expected it."

A bolt from the blue (also: a thunderbolt from the blue)
Meaning: A sudden, shocking, completely unexpected event — usually an unpleasant one. Stronger in feel than "out of the blue" — this one emphasizes the shock.

  • "His sudden resignation was a bolt from the blue."

Blue in the face
Meaning: Exhausted and frustrated from trying very hard — talking, arguing, explaining, or doing something — without any success or result.

  • "I argued with him until I was blue in the face, but he refused to change his mind."
  • "You can explain the instructions until you're blue in the face — she won't follow them."

Into the blue
Meaning: Disappearing into an unknown, distant, or uncertain place; going somewhere that cannot be tracked or known.

  • "He packed his bags and vanished into the blue."

Scream/shout blue murder (mainly British English)
Meaning: To protest, complain, or shout extremely loudly and angrily.

  • "When the council announced the new road, local residents screamed blue murder."

Talk a blue streak (mainly American English)
Meaning: To talk extremely fast and at great length without stopping.

  • "Once she gets started, she talks a blue streak — you can barely get a word in."

Between the devil and the deep blue sea
Meaning: Caught in a situation where both available choices are bad; trapped in a dilemma with no good way out.

  • "I could tell my boss the truth and get fired, or stay silent and feel guilty. I was between the devil and the deep blue sea."

• Color — the color of a clear sky or the sea; ranges from pale baby blue to deep navy blue
  • Emotional — sad, melancholy, low in spirits
  • Content — crude, sexually suggestive, adult in nature
  • Political (US) — Democratic; (UK) — Conservative
  • Physical — skin turning bluish from cold or lack of oxygen
  • Moral/Legal — excessively strict, puritanical (blue laws)
  • Social class — aristocratic, noble (blue blood, blue-blooded)
  • Compound forms — blue-collar (manual labor), blue-chip (top-quality and reliable), true blue (deeply loyal), blue-eyed boy/girl (a favorite)
  • Idioms — once in a blue moon (rarely), out of the blue (unexpectedly), blue in the face (exhausted from trying), a bolt from the blue (sudden shock), talk a blue streak (talk non-stop), between the devil and the deep blue sea (stuck between two bad options)
1918:
When you do something "until you are blue in the face," it means you do it for a very long time, repeatedly, and with great effort — but it makes no difference. The result does not change. Nobody listens. Nothing works. All that effort is completely wasted.

The idiom is about pointless, exhausting effort that goes nowhere.
The Full Form of the Idiom

You will almost always see this idiom written as:

"until you are blue in the face"
or
"till you are blue in the face"

It is rarely just "blue in the face" on its own. The word "until" is the key — it sets up the idea of doing something endlessly, right up to the extreme limit of physical exhaustion.

The image behind this idiom is very physical and very real.

Think about what happens to a person who screams, cries, argues, or holds their breath for an extremely long time. Their body runs low on oxygen. When the human body is severely starved of oxygen, the skin — especially on the face — can turn a bluish or purplish color. Doctors call this cyanosis. You may have seen a baby turn blue from crying too hard, or a person's lips turn blue from extreme cold or exertion.

So the idiom paints this picture: imagine someone arguing so hard, for so long, that their face literally turns blue from the effort. That is how extreme and exhausting the action is. And yet — even after all that — nothing changes.

The idiom has been used in English for well over a hundred years and is well established in both British and American English.
How to Use It — The Grammar

The idiom follows a very consistent pattern. Study this structure:

Subject + can + [verb/action] + until + [they are] + blue in the face

The verb before "until" describes the action that is being done pointlessly.

Here are clear examples across different situations:

1. Arguing / Debating

"You can argue with him until you are blue in the face, but he will never admit he is wrong."

(No matter how long or how hard you argue, it will not work.)

2. Explaining / Teaching

"The teacher explained the rule until she was blue in the face, but the students still did not understand."

(She explained it over and over, exhausting herself, but it made no difference.)

3. Complaining

"He complained to the company until he was blue in the face. They never responded."

(He complained endlessly, but nothing came of it.)

4. Asking / Requesting

"I can ask my boss for a raise until I am blue in the face — she is never going to say yes."

(No matter how many times I ask, the answer will not change.)

5. Warning someone

"You can warn her until you are blue in the face. She will still make her own choices."

(Your warnings, no matter how many, will not change her behavior.)

This idiom carries a strong feeling of frustration and resignation. When someone uses it, they are usually expressing one of two things:

A) The speaker is dismissing someone else's effort:
When you say "You can talk until you're blue in the face," you are telling that person: "Save your breath. It won't work. I won't change. Nothing will change." There is a slightly cold, dismissive tone here.

B) The speaker is expressing their own exhaustion and frustration:
When you say "I tried to explain it until I was blue in the face," you are expressing how tired and frustrated you are because nobody listened to you, no matter how hard you tried.

Many idioms about effort — like "give it your best shot" or "go the extra mile" — suggest that effort is rewarded. This idiom is the opposite. It specifically highlights situations where effort is not rewarded. It assumes from the start that the effort is futile. This makes it a very honest, blunt, and sometimes slightly bitter expression.

Mistake 1: Leaving out "until"
❌ "She was blue in the face explaining it."
✅ "She explained it until she was blue in the face."

The "until" is what creates the meaning of endless, prolonged effort. Without it, the phrase sounds incomplete or odd.

Mistake 2: Using it for effort that actually succeeds
This idiom is specifically for futile effort. If someone eventually got the result they wanted, this idiom does not fit.

❌ "He practiced until he was blue in the face and finally won the championship."
✅ "He practiced until he was blue in the face, but he still lost every match."

Mistake 3: Taking it too literally
Nobody's face is actually turning blue. It is a figurative expression. The "blue face" is simply an exaggerated image of extreme, exhausting effort.
Register and Tone — When Is It Used?

This idiom is informal to semi-formal. You will hear it in:

  • Everyday conversation between friends or family
  • Casual writing, blogs, and opinion pieces
  • Workplace discussions (but in relaxed settings, not formal reports)

You would not typically use it in highly formal academic writing or official documents.

Knowing related idioms helps you understand the full picture:

  • "Talking to a wall" — making no impact, because the other person is not listening at all.
  • "Flogging a dead horse" — wasting time on something that has no hope of working.
  • "In one ear and out the other" — something is heard but immediately ignored or forgotten.
  • "Beating a dead horse" (American version of the above)
  • "Save your breath" — don't even bother speaking, because it will make no difference.

All of these share the theme of wasted effort, but "blue in the face" is unique because it emphasizes the physical exhaustion and duration of that effort more vividly than the others.
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

Core meaningDoing something repeatedly and exhaustively, with absolutely no result
Feeling it expressesFrustration, futility, exasperation
Key word"Until" — the effort goes on and on
Used forArguing, explaining, complaining, asking, warning
StyleInformal, blunt, sometimes dismissive
What it is NOT aboutSuccessful effort — it always implies failure or being ignored

The next time you see someone trying to convince a stubborn person, or repeating themselves endlessly to no effect, you now have the perfect idiom: they are doing it until they are blue in the face.
1919:
When you call something blue-collar, you are describing work, workers, or anything connected to jobs that primarily involve physical or manual labor, skilled trades, or operating machinery. Think of the people who build your house, repair your car, wire your electricity, assemble products in a factory, drive delivery trucks, mine coal, lay down roads, or fix your plumbing. All of these are blue-collar jobs.

The word is the opposite of white-collar, which describes office-based, desk-based, or professional work — like lawyers, accountants, managers, and bankers. This contrast is the single most important thing to understand about the word, because "blue-collar" almost always carries its meaning relative to that distinction.

As an adjective, "blue-collar" can attach itself to many different nouns:

  • A blue-collar worker — a person whose job involves physical labor or a manual trade.
  • A blue-collar job — a position in construction, manufacturing, transportation, mining, plumbing, electrical work, welding, carpentry, and so on.
  • A blue-collar industry — an entire sector built on physical work, like the steel industry or the trucking industry.
  • A blue-collar town/neighborhood — a community where most residents work in factories, plants, or trades, and where the local economy depends on those industries.
  • Blue-collar values — an attitude associated with hard work, practicality, toughness, and a no-nonsense approach to life.
  • Blue-collar roots — a person's background or upbringing in a working-class, physically-laboring family or community.

So the adjective is flexible. It can describe people, places, jobs, industries, attitudes, and even cultures.

Not all blue-collar work is the same. It ranges widely:

  • Skilled trades — electricians, plumbers, welders, carpenters, and mechanics. These require years of specialized training, apprenticeships, or certifications. They demand real expertise.
  • Semi-skilled labor — operating specific machines in a factory, driving large vehicles, or working on an assembly line. These require some training but less than a full trade.
  • Unskilled or general labor — jobs like basic construction labor, warehouse work, or sanitation, which require physical effort and minimal formal training.

All three fall under the "blue-collar" umbrella, but a skilled electrician and a general laborer are very different in terms of expertise and earnings.

This is important for sharp accuracy:

  • It does not automatically mean low-paid. Many skilled tradespeople — plumbers, electricians, welders — earn very competitive, sometimes excellent, salaries. The assumption that blue-collar = poor is a stereotype, not a definition.
  • It does not mean uneducated. Blue-collar workers often undergo rigorous technical training, apprenticeships, and certifications. Their education is just more hands-on and vocational rather than academic.
  • It does not mean simple or unimportant. Society depends entirely on blue-collar workers. Without them, buildings don't get built, pipes don't get fixed, food doesn't get delivered, and electricity doesn't flow.

A word's connotation is the emotional or social feeling it carries beyond its strict definition. "Blue-collar" has a nuanced set of connotations:

  • Pride and respect: Many people use "blue-collar" with pride. Saying "I come from a blue-collar family" often signals a respect for hard work, humility, and practical skills.
  • Working-class identity: The term is closely tied to the concept of the working class — people who earn wages through labor rather than through managing capital or sitting behind a desk. Blue-collar workers have historically been associated with labor unions, collective bargaining, and workers' rights movements.
  • Occasional condescension: In some contexts, unfortunately, "blue-collar" has been used dismissively to imply lower social status. This is a misuse rooted in cultural bias, not in the word's actual meaning.
  • The "hardworking, no-frills" image: When used metaphorically (see below), it almost always suggests someone or something that relies on effort and grit rather than glamour or polish.

Because of its association with hard work and practicality, "blue-collar" is sometimes used metaphorically — beyond the literal world of jobs — to describe a style or attitude:

  • "A blue-collar athlete" — a sports player who may not have the most dazzling natural talent, but outworks everyone around them. They grind. They show up. They earn their place through relentless effort rather than raw genius.
  • "A blue-collar approach" — a straightforward, practical, no-nonsense way of doing something. No unnecessary flair, just focused execution.
  • "A blue-collar performance" — in a game, a concert, or any endeavor, a performance that wasn't flashy but was solid, reliable, and built on hard work.

In these uses, the adjective pays a sincere compliment. It praises effort, durability, and work ethic.

Here are sentences using "blue-collar" as an adjective, showing its range:

  1. "She grew up in a blue-collar family — her father worked at the steel mill for thirty years."
  2. "The city's economy had long depended on blue-collar jobs in manufacturing."
  3. "The new policy was designed to ease the financial burden on blue-collar workers."
  4. "It's a blue-collar town, and the people there are proud of it."
  5. "He may not be the most talented player on the team, but he has a blue-collar mentality that the coach loves."
  6. "Blue-collar industries like construction and transportation were hit hardest by the supply chain disruptions."

"Blue-collar" describes work, workers, places, and attitudes associated with physical labor, manual trades, and working-class identity — as opposed to office-based or professional work — and often carries connotations of hard work, practicality, and working-class pride.
